# BSCCM overview figures: what each panel shows and says

**Common to all figures.**
- Bars show the mean. Whiskers are 1 SD. Hollow rings are the individual values (seeds, donors, teachers or slides, as stated per figure).
- Stars come from two-sided paired t-tests against the grey reference bar, Holm-corrected within each panel. "ns" means p ≥ .05.

**GOAL.** GOAL is the main score of the project.
- Task: predict each cell's surface-marker level from its label-free images (multi-illumination LED-array microscopy).
- Training and test: train on one blood draw, test on the other.
- Score: Pearson r between predicted and measured level, averaged over 11 targets:
  - 8 single markers: CD16, CD14, CD45, CD3, CD123, CD56, HLA-DR, CD19;
  - 3 pooled antibody panels: CD3/CD19/CD56, CD45, CD16;
  - then averaged over both directions (draw 1 → 0 and 0 → 1).
- Target: .70. Seed noise: SD .0027.

---

## Figure 1: Progress of the GOAL over the project (`fig1_progress`)

**a. Single networks.** Each ring is the best single-network result of one notebook item (mean over seeds where several were run). The step line is the best so far.
- Colour marks the label version the value was scored on: v5 (N023–N050) or v10 (N051 onwards). Each change of label version re-bases all numbers, so a jump between colours is not model progress.
- On v5, single networks rose from .640 (N023) to .653 (N040, noisy-student pseudo-labels).
- On v10 they rose from .673 (N051) to .677 (N063, two-part output head with per-field-of-view offsets, seeds 2–3).
- About 15 later single-network ideas all landed at .662–.676.

**b. Multi-network results.** Each ring is an item's primary (planned) ensemble or composite.
- On v10 the GOAL record is .6862 (N053: ResNet-50 base + 2× zoom + Cytoland encoder; replicated with a fresh seed at .6864).
- Later combinations reached .690–.691, including the pre-registered N084 at .6911. All stayed below the improvement threshold of .6916 (record + 2 × noise).
- Descriptive secondary combinations reached up to .6929 (N065); they are not counted.
- The dashed line is the .70 target.

**Says:** most of the gain came from better labels (v5 → v10) and ensembling diverse encoders. Single networks have stayed flat at about .67 since N051, and the best ensemble is about .01 short of .70.

## Figure 2: What was tried: single-network changes vs a matched control (`fig2_attempts`)

Every panel shows the change in GOAL against the same ResNet-50 control (in-domain self-supervised pretraining), compared seed by seed (control .6730 / .6683). Rings are seeds.

**a. Output heads.**

| Head | Change in GOAL |
|---|---|
| HL-Gauss classification head | −.012 |
| two-part head (positive / negative) | +.005 |
| panel head | ±.000 |
| Pearson-correlation loss | +.002 |

**b. Losses and sampling.**

| Change | Change in GOAL |
|---|---|
| per-field-of-view offsets | +.003 |
| pair loss | +.004 |
| no autofluorescence target | +.001 |
| field-of-view-balanced sampler | −.007 |

**c. Labels and supervision.**

| Change | Change in GOAL |
|---|---|
| consensus labels | −.008 |
| label separation | ±.000 |
| censored loss + 20 epochs | −.005 |
| auxiliary fluorescence-image decoder | −.002 |
| multi-marker fine-tune | −.003 |
| symmetry augmentation | −.001 |

**d. Encoders and data.** ConvNeXt-S with in-domain pretraining −.003, Cytoland −.005. Single-seed arms, so no test:

| Arm | Change in GOAL |
|---|---|
| Cytoland at full learning rate | −.027 |
| DINOv3-B | −.022 |
| DINOv3-S | −.024 |
| DinoBloom-B | −.018 |
| ResNet-50 with 4× longer pretraining | −.002 |
| + ImageStream external data | −.006 |

**Says:** no change to the head, loss, labels or encoder moved a single network beyond seed noise; every test is ns. Generic pretrained vision encoders are clearly worse than in-domain self-supervised pretraining.

## Figure 3: Where the remaining error is (`fig3_gap`)

**a. Per-target r.** Mean over both directions for four models:
- ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-S, each the mean of seeds 0 and 1;
- the N053 ensemble;
- the N084 ensemble.

Bright lineage markers are predicted well: CD16 about .90, CD14, CD3, CD45 and the pooled panels about .70–.85. Four dim markers carry most of the error: CD19 .35, HLA-DR .47, CD56 .52, CD123 .56. The ranking is the same for every model.

**b. Per direction (N084 ensemble).** Draw 0 → 1 (trained on the smaller draw) is weaker overall: .679 vs .703. The main losses are on CD123 (.54 vs .65), HLA-DR and the pooled CD45 panel.

**c. Learning curve at matched training steps (N082, seed 0).**
- 50 % of training labels, 10 epochs: .646.
- 50 %, 20 epochs: .658.
- 100 %, 10 epochs: .673.

At the same number of training steps, twice the labelled cells gives +.016 (.673 vs .658). Twice the steps on the same half gives only +.012 (.658 vs .646). The model is limited by labels, not by optimisation.

**d. Label agreement.** Agreement between the v10 labels and an independently derived label version (local background subtraction) on the held-out cells. Rings are directions.
- CD19 agrees only .32 and CD56 .71, so their labels are unstable.
- The other targets agree at .81 or more.
- High agreement does not prove the labels are correct: CD123 agrees .89 but is still predicted at only .54–.65.

**Says:** the error is concentrated in a few dim markers. For CD19 and CD56 the labels themselves are unreliable, and more labelled cells would help more than longer training.

## Figure 4: Decoding all markers of a cell jointly (`fig4_multimarker`)

**a. BSCCM pooled-panel score (MM3).** MM3 is the mean r of the three pooled antibody panels. ConvNeXt-S (in-domain pretraining) scores .771 vs .758 for ResNet-50.
- The gain (+.0135) cleared the pre-registered bar (+.007) on both seeds.
- With only 2 seeds the paired t-test is ns.

**b–f** use the external imaging-flow-cytometry dataset S-BIAD452.
- It has 274,050 cells from 3 donors, with 9 markers measured on every cell.
- The models see only the brightfield and side-scatter channels.
- Three training regimes are compared:
  - **all 9 markers** labelled on each cell;
  - **one marker per cell**, as in BSCCM's single-stain slides;
  - **one marker per cell + pooled panels** on 10 % of cells.
- Each donor is held out once; rings are donors.

**b. Mean r over the 9 markers.** All 9 markers .596, one marker per cell .526, + pooled .542.
- The cell-type oracle reaches .814. It gives each cell the average marker profile of its true (gated) cell type.

**c. Per-marker r.**
- All-marker training beats single-marker training on every one of the 9 markers. The largest gains are on CD4 (.52 vs .36) and CD15 (.86 vs .77).
- CD8, CD56 and CD19 are worst in every regime (.26–.43).
- The oracle's CD4/CD8 values are high partly because T-cell subsets are gated by CD4 and CD8 themselves.

**d. Correlations between marker pairs within a population** (averaged over donors).
- CD4–CD8 within T cells: measured −.81. Predicted −.36 (all markers), −.07 (one marker), +.16 (pooled).
- CD3–CD19 within lymphocytes: measured −.73. All regimes predict −.83 to −.89.
- CD3–CD56 and CD19–CD56: weak, and similar across regimes.

**e. Pre-registered co-expression error.** Mean |predicted − measured| correlation over all 36 marker pairs on whole donors: all markers .189, one marker .229, pooled .237 (ns).

**f. Within-cell-type r.** Pearson r inside each gated cell type: .20 / .18 / .15.

**Says:** labelling every cell with all markers gives better per-marker decoding (+.07). It also reproduces co-expression better, most clearly the CD4/CD8 exclusivity that single-stain training loses. No regime differs significantly with 3 donors. The bigger limit is that these images mostly encode cell type: decoding within a cell type is weak in every regime, and models fall short even of the cell-type oracle.

## Figure 5: Giemsa → markers via the label-free bridge (`fig5_giemsa`)

Students that read Giemsa-stained blood images are trained from the label-free model. They are evaluated on the external MLL23 clinical smear set, as AUROC over pre-registered fine cell-type contrasts. In panels a–b, rings are 3 label-free teacher models, each the mean of its 2–3 student seeds; tests are paired by teacher.

**a. Distillation target.**
- Distilling the teacher's latent "hub" representation gives .681 AUROC. Distilling its marker outputs gives .568.
- The teacher-paired test gives p = .07.
- Under the pre-registered rule (mean gain .113 > seed noise floor .074) the hub counts as better. The per-teacher gains were +.061, +.109 and +.169.

**b. Anchoring strength for output distillation** (class-anchor weight .5 / 2 / 8): .568 / .604 / .627. This is a trend only, ns; the pre-registered rule says no difference.

**c. Three-way latent designs (N054).** Same-cell autofluorescence r on the 2 held-out slides (rings).
- Output distillation .658, label-free hub .650, direct map .647.
- Two-space design with label-free flow .642, with Giemsa flow .625.
- Unpaired Gromov–Wasserstein alignment .32.

**Says:** distilling a shared latent representation transfers better to clinical Giemsa smears than distilling marker outputs. The two-space design does as well as the hub. Alignment without paired cells fails.

---

## Figure 6: Architecture of the best model (`fig6_architecture`), written for ML readers

**Task.** Per-cell multi-output regression.
- Input: one cell imaged with a programmable LED-array microscope. There are 23 illumination patterns (brightfield, darkfield rings at increasing angles, half-circle phase-contrast patterns and single LEDs) plus one computed phase image, stacked into a 24 × 128 × 128 tensor.
- Output: 13 regression targets (protein levels); 11 of them are scored.

**Main difficulty: sparse labels.** Training uses a masked MSE over the observed targets only.
- Cells from single-stain slides have 1 protein target plus 1 background (autofluorescence) target.
- Cells from pooled-panel slides have 4 (draw 0) or 3 (draw 1) pooled targets and no background target.

**Evaluation.** Train on one blood draw, test on the other (a domain shift). Score = Pearson r, averaged over 11 targets and both directions.

**Model: an ensemble of 4 separately trained members.** Each member is an image encoder → global pooling → linear heads; test predictions are averaged.
1. ResNet-50 (23.6 M parameters, 2048-d features), full 128 px view.
2. ResNet-50, 2× centre zoom.
3. ConvNeXtV2-T (27.9 M, 768-d), initialised from the encoder of a published microscopy image-to-image model (Cytoland). Its 1-channel stem is repeated to 24, it has a learned per-channel gain, and it is fine-tuned at 0.1× the learning rate.
4. ConvNeXt-S (49.5 M, 768-d).

**Self-supervised init (members 1, 2, 4).**
- 2 augmented views (random scale and shift), invariance loss plus the SIGReg Gaussian regulariser.
- Runs on unlabelled cells of the training split only.
- 40 epochs for ResNet-50; 60–120 epochs for ConvNeXt-S.

**Heads and fine-tuning.**
- Linear regression head (13 outputs).
- Auxiliary 3- and 10-class cell-type heads (cross-entropy, weight 0.5). Their labels exist only for pooled-panel cells of draw 0, and they are not used at test time.
- Fine-tuning: 10 epochs, AdamW, lr 5e-4, batch 256, ±4 px random shift. No rotations or flips, because the illumination channels are direction-dependent.

**Score.** GOAL .6911 (pre-registered, N084), just below the .6916 improvement threshold.
- The GOAL record, N053, is the first three members (.6862; .6864 with the Cytoland member re-trained on a fresh seed).
- A 6-member combination registered in N065 as a descriptive secondary analysis reached .6929; it is not counted toward the GOAL.

## Figure 7: Architectures compared (`fig7_architectures`)

**a. Single encoders.** Same data, labels and heads for every encoder; rings are seeds; paired t-tests against ResNet-50 for the arms with 2 seeds.

| Encoder | Initialisation | GOAL |
|---|---|---|
| ResNet-50 | our self-supervised pretraining | .671 |
| ResNet-50, 4× longer pretraining | our self-supervised pretraining | .671 |
| ConvNeXt-S | our self-supervised pretraining | .668 (ns) |
| ConvNeXtV2-T | published microscopy model (Cytoland) | .666 (ns) |
| ConvNeXtV2-T, full learning rate | published microscopy model (Cytoland) | .646 |
| ViT-B | blood-smear photos (DinoBloom) | .655 |
| ViT-B | natural images (DINOv3) | .651 |
| ViT-S | natural images (DINOv3) | .649 |

The arms also differ in fine-tuning learning rate, input resolution (ViTs at 224–256 px) and pooling. This panel compares complete recipes; it does not isolate the pretraining source.

**b. Ensembles** (mean of member predictions):
- ResNet-50 alone: .674.
- Full view + 2× zoom pair: .680. Both ResNet-50 arms were trained on the cf150 label variant; trained on v10 labels they score .673 and .679.
- Adding a third member:
  - a ViT: .680–.682;
  - Cytoland: .686, the registered record.
- Adding ConvNeXt-S as a fourth member: .691.

Seed noise SD is .0027.

**Says:**
- In this comparison, CNNs initialised by self-supervised pretraining on our own unlabelled cells are the best single encoders. Generic ViTs, even with nearly 4× more parameters, are .015–.021 lower, with the recipe caveats above.
- Among our self-supervised CNNs the architecture hardly matters.
- Ensembles gain most from members with a different pretraining source (Cytoland) or architecture (ConvNeXt-S). ViT members add almost nothing.

---

## Figure 8: Aligning two image modalities of the same cells (`fig8_alignment_crossmodal`), written for ML readers

**Setup.** The same blood cells exist in two image modalities:
- label-free microscope stacks (LF), on which the marker predictor is trained;
- photos of the same cells after Giemsa staining (GS), the format hospitals use.

There are 15.7k registered cell pairs on 2 slides. The aim is to make LF-trained predictions available from GS images. Every test is on a held-out slide; rings are the two slides (b1: 5,697 cells; b0: 10,015 cells), one seed each.

**a. Exact-cell retrieval GS → LF on the held-out slide (R@10).** Chance is .0018 / .0010; dashed line .0018.
- Linear map (ridge regression GS → LF features fitted on the pairs): .013.
- CCA: .017. Procrustes: .016.
- SigLIP contrastive: .030.
- SOTAlign (SigLIP plus optimal transport on unpaired clinical GS and LF cells): .028.
- Across slides, every method stays at .01–.04.
- Within a slide (held-out fields of view, chance .010–.016), the same SigLIP and SOTAlign models reach R@10 .38–.40.
- Caveat (literature review N088, check pending): paired images share their field of view (background, focus) and there are only ~3 paired cells per field, so part of the within-slide score may come from recognising the field rather than the cell. The cross-slide number is the trustworthy one.

**b. Transferring a per-cell signal.** The signal is a scalar measured on both slides (autofluorescence); the score is r against its measured value on the held-out cells. Each bar is a complete pipeline.
- Embedding plus ridge readout: .21–.40 (CCA .21, SigLIP .28, SOTAlign .33, Procrustes .40). The linear map gives .57.
- GS students trained to regress the LF model's outputs (output distillation) or its latent: .66 (.715 / .601) and .65 (.751 / .549).
- A two-space model whose final alignment step is unpaired Gromov–Wasserstein: .32 (.18 / .46). Its GS encoder was itself trained with pairs.
- The pipelines differ in more than the alignment step. For example, the student pipelines' LF training also saw unstained cells of the held-out slide.

**c. Learning from set-level supervision with the pairs hidden.** The LF → label map is learned only from matched sets of cells. Per-cell r on a new blood draw is plotted against set size; the dashed line is the fully paired readout (.561).
- This is one draw, with features from an encoder that also saw the test draw.
- Sets of the same cells recover most of the signal at 4–16 cells (.55 / .50) and decay towards .10 at 2,048.
- 1-D OT collapses beyond 64 cells.
- Sets of different cells carry no per-cell information (r ≈ 0).

**Says:**
- Joint embeddings retrieve cells within a slide (possibly helped by a field-of-view shortcut, check pending) but not on a new slide.
- For carrying a per-cell signal from LF to GS, directly distilling the LF model into a GS network beat every embedding-plus-readout pipeline we ran.
- Without paired cells, only small sets of the same cells give useful supervision.

## Figure 9: Domain-shift methods (`fig9_alignment_domain`)

**a–b. Clinical smears.** A Giemsa-reading network trained on our cells is applied to public clinical smear datasets from other labs, stains and cameras. The score is the AUROC of pre-registered cell-class contrasts; 0.5 is chance.

**a. PBC dataset.** Rings are the 8 contrasts; paired t-tests against no adaptation.
- No adaptation: .41.
- Test-time whitening: .44.
- Domain-adversarial training (DANN on unlabelled PBC images): .46 at λ = .1, .55 at λ = .3.

All are ns, and individual contrasts range from .11 to .90.

**b. MLL23 dataset.** Rings are 3 teacher models; paired t-tests by teacher. All arms use class anchoring: a cross-entropy on 3 common classes from labelled PBC images.
- Output distillation: .568.
- Post-hoc alignment of the clinical features:
  - unbalanced OT .562, mean shift .571, CORAL .571 (ns);
  - single teachers move by up to −.038;
  - these arms decode an aligned mean embedding rather than averaging decoded predictions.

# work-log protocol

## Containment (hard)
- All under `<repo>/.agent-research/` — hidden, committed. `notebook/` = index + knowledge;
  `results/N###-slug/` = that entry's outputs. Never `.claude/` or `.agents/`.
- Every figure, table, CSV, log excerpt, one-off script or report goes in that `results/`
  folder; only real project code goes elsewhere.
- Outputs >5 MB stay where produced, referenced by absolute path
  (`notebook/META.md` large_output_location).
- Exception: comparison plots → `.agent-research/plots/<metric>_<date>.png`.
- Hidden dir: ALWAYS explicit `.agent-research/` paths in Glob/Grep/scripts.

## When to log
Only work producing a commit, result, decision or non-obvious lesson, or >~10 tool calls.

## Before
`bin/new-item.sh <type> "<title>"` — exp task fix research analysis writing decision review.
Creates `notebook/items/N###-slug.md` + `results/N###-slug/` + an INDEX row (`open`).

## During
All outputs into that results folder. Experiment: a stated hypothesis with an expected result, a named baseline (the current best), a
kill criterion — before launching; an attempt may change several things at once. Screen on 1 seed
(bar = 2 x noise); >= 3-seed replication at the end of each MAJOR accomplishment. ONE `exp` item per hypothesis. A TRAINING run gets its item AT
SUBMIT (job id, config/branch, gpus x time, log path) and must be registered in wandb with
its job id in the sync lineage — compute nodes have no internet, the login cron is the only
path.
Save every measured value (long csv/json `arm,seed,metric,value[,x]`) here; plot each comparison:
`bin/plot-compare --metric M --csv F --item N### --baseline A`, cite the png (`effect.sh` checks both).
Jobs: preempt + `bin/preempt-run.sh`; GPU-h = rough estimate, no measuring jobs.

## After
1. Fill the item; update the INDEX row (status, one-line outcome, commit hash); append to
   `notebook/log.jsonl`. Closing an attempt at a goal: `bin/effect.sh N### improved|flat|worse|n/a
   [--value V] [--scale knob|module|paradigm]` (improved counts only if it beats GOAL.md best by
   more than its noise; an unlabelled closed exp counts as flat).
2. A result killing a prior belief goes to KNOWLEDGE `## Refuted` with what killed it —
   refutations are findings, never dropped.
3. Edit KNOWLEDGE only if understanding changed — single bullets, never a rewrite:
   `K###: <finding|decision|gotcha> [verified|partial|unverified] (N###; path) {cites:n}`
4. Follow-ups → `notebook/TODO.md`.
5. Every number or claim cites its source (path, command, URL). No source, no claim.

## Housekeeping (advisory)
Mind the `QUOTA` line; clean up every few turns. `.sif` envs, packed data; big → `/hnvme`, small temp → home subdir,
deleted at end; drop stale logs/caches/old ckpts. ORCHESTRATION.md 'Housekeeping'.

## Lint and review
`LINT DUE` from `state.sh`/`new-item.sh` → run `work-lint` immediately, without asking.
`REVIEW DUE` (stall guard: 5 flat attempts in a row vs `notebook/GOAL.md`; `new-item.sh` refuses
exp|task|fix|analysis) → run `work-review` at once. New goal-driven project → `bin/goal.sh init` first.
Details: ORCHESTRATION.md 'Stall guard'.

## Commits, branches, PRs
- Commit ONLY a coherent block (submodule/feature/fix) that is DONE and that control AND
  red-team passed — not mid-change. Code + its `.agent-research/` records in ONE commit,
  `N###: <summary>`; hash into the INDEX row.
- NEVER commit or push on default/main. Working branch only; push per finished block.
- PR gate: list EVERY pipeline the change touches, each with its exact command and exit
  status. Unlisted = unverified = PR blocked. Each must RUN TO COMPLETION on GPU (when GPU
  conditioning is enabled) AND on CPU; GPU-only if the branch clearly profits from GPU.
  Imports and pytest are the writer's job and do NOT count here.
- The PR states the changes and that evidence; resolve every conflict.
- Merges into main are the USER's, by hand. Never merge, never auto-merge.

## Agents — reader + writer per job, cross-model review always
Order: reader -> writer -> control ‖ cross-review. Both reviewers also apply retroactively to
existing code. Keep the source READ-ONLY.
- **While a run is going:** explore — new angles, alternative approaches, agents, cheap tests, `notebook/IDEAS.md`; no idling. ORCHESTRATION.md 'While a job runs'.
- **Several problems at a time:** bundle separable problems into one attempt (no one-variable rule); agents are optional help, never a quota; subagents never own jobs > ~10 min. ORCHESTRATION.md 'Several problems at a time'.
- **reader** (Claude) — studies the source, writes an in-depth implementation spec. No code.
- **writer** (Claude OR Codex) — implements from that spec. Default to Codex for large/bulk/
  high-context jobs (ports, multi-file changes, long reads) — it keeps that reading out of
  Claude's context entirely. Keep small, quick edits with Claude: a Codex job round-trip
  costs more turns than writing three lines. Codex writes only into
  `results/N###-slug/codex/`, never the live tree.
- **control** (**Claude Opus**, or a script) — reads BOTH implementations, checks
  equivalence and, for geometric models, equivariance. Independence comes from the METHOD,
  not the model — so same-family is right and a script is better. Unaffected by who wrote it.
- **cross-review (red-team)** — whichever model did NOT write it: Codex red-teams Claude's
  code, Claude red-teams Codex's landed code (`/code-review` or a general-purpose subagent,
  same adversarial brief either direction). Independence comes from PRIORS; same-family
  review regenerates the same blind spots. Mandatory before anything is acted on or marked
  `[verified]` — not scoped to high-stakes jobs only.
- **integrator** (Claude) — checks Codex's code in `results/N###-slug/codex/` against the
  real tree, adapts it to local conventions, lands it. The only agent that lands Codex code.
- **Two-strike loop** is one trigger among several for routing a job to Codex, not the only
  one: after TWO failed Claude attempts, stop retrying. Codex root-causes, then writes AND
  tests a fix in `results/N###-slug/codex/` — never the live tree — and delivers it with the
  plan. The integrator lands it; Claude then cross-reviews what LANDED. Still broken?
  Repeat, handing Codex every prior round so it gives new ideas.
- **Never act on a reviewer's finding until you reproduce it.** Reviewers REPORT; the main
  agent decides. Reproduce the failure, confound or trivial baseline from the cited
  file/line/command. Confirmed -> fix. Not reproducible -> `[unverified]` with why, and NO
  code change. "Nothing breaks" is likewise not proof — one search that found nothing.
- **Never trust a Codex job's `completed` status** — it is recorded even when the sandbox
  ran no command. Launch with `bin/codex-run.sh` (self-gating; OK or CODEX-UNAVAILABLE), or gate a plugin job with `bin/codex-check.sh <job-id>`. On
  `CODEX-UNAVAILABLE`, fall back to Claude for whichever side (write or review) Codex was
  doing, and note "same-family (codex unavailable)" in the item.
- Only the main agent writes to `notebook/`. Subagents return <=2k tokens and write outputs
  ONLY into the item's `results/` folder — give each its path explicitly.
- Keep records out of auto memory. Contracts + the cross-review prompt: ORCHESTRATION.md.

## Ambiguity
Take the most reversible option, log it in `notebook/SETUP_NOTES.md`, continue. Stop only
if data would be deleted or overwritten.
# Agent orchestration — who reads what, when

## Context is the scarce resource
The main agent's context is the only thing surviving a whole task. Anything entering it that
the next decision does not need is waste; subagents keep large reads OUT. Parallel agents are
OPTIONAL help — use them where independent work exists and they run reliably, never as a quota.

## Read order, any non-trivial task
1. `bin/state.sh` — RULES, last 10 INDEX rows, KNOWLEDGE headline, open TODOs. Always,
   <=25 lines.
2. Only if a row/bullet is relevant: grep that item file or results folder. Never the
   whole notebook. One flat level: INDEX/KNOWLEDGE -> one detail file.
3. Project code: only the files the task touches.
Never re-read what an earlier turn established. The notebook is the memory; re-deriving is
the failure it exists to prevent.

## When to delegate
When the ANSWER is small but the READING is large: sweeping files, scanning logs, surveying
a library, checking a claim across a codebase — OR when the work is independent of what you
are doing now. Not what you can do in two tool calls, and never the judgment itself —
a subagent proposes, the main agent decides.

## Several problems at a time
Do not work one problem per attempt. When the diagnosis shows several separable problems, address them
together: bundle the changes in one attempt (baseline = the current best; ablate only what wins) or run
separate items side by side when the cluster allows. There is no one-variable rule. Reliability rules
that stay (observed failures):
- **Subagents do not own long jobs.** A Bash call tops out at 10 minutes, so a subagent that backgrounds a
  GPU job and returns delivers nothing (2026-10-07: a diagnostic agent "stopped once more on its own
  background GPU work"). For a job > ~10 min the subagent returns a ready-to-submit package; the
  coordinator submits and owns the `wait-job.sh` waiter.
- **Blocked on the user (>25 GPU-h yes, a decision) blocks that item, not the session:** ask in chat, keep
  the other work going.
- **Ending a turn** only when every pending job/agent has a harness-tracked waiter (re-arm one lost in a
  session restart) — otherwise the user has to type "go on".

## While a job runs: no idling
Any long-running work (training run, build, download, agent task) is the moment to widen the search, not to wait. Typical order (do what pays, skip the rest):
1. Read the run's early signals against the stated expectation (cheap; do not touch the job).
2. Ideate: 3-5 NEW angles on the goal — different mechanisms, data, representations, decompositions, framings — not tweaks of the
   running job. Wild or contrarian ideas are explicitly welcome. One line each in `notebook/IDEAS.md`
   (`idea · mechanism · cheapest test · status open|testing|promising|dead(why)`).
3. Agents: literature on the open question, a Codex idea-writer, an outsider or assumption-breaker (the `work-review` step-3
   briefs, lighter). Reports into the item's `agents/` folder.
4. Test the best ideas as far as cheap means allow before any real investment: CPU analyses, ceiling/oracle tests, tiny prototypes,
   cached features, offline evaluation of existing checkpoints, small GPU jobs inside the budget rules (>25 GPU-h still needs a yes;
   GPU only if >=2x a CPU run). Do not compete with the running job for its GPUs.
5. Prepare the next package (pre-registration, scripts, evaluation) so nothing waits when the run ends.
6. Record: promising -> `new-item.sh exp "<title>" module|paradigm`; dead -> IDEAS.md with the reason (and KNOWLEDGE `## Refuted` if it kills a belief).
Quality over quantity: an idea that is only a hyper-parameter of the running job does not count. The stall gate still applies to new
exp items. Ending a turn with a run going is fine once this is done (or there is nothing useful left — say so in the last message).

## The five roles (each names WHO runs it)
Order: reader -> writer -> control ‖ cross-review -> (integrator, when Codex supplied code).
Both reviewers also apply retroactively. Keep the source READ-ONLY.
- **reader** — Claude, read-only. Studies the source, writes an in-depth implementation
  spec, cites paths, <=2k tokens. Never edits.
- **writer** — **Claude OR Codex**. Implements from that spec. Default to Codex for
  large/bulk/high-context jobs — ports, multi-file changes, long reads — because keeping
  that reading entirely out of Claude's context is the real token-efficiency win: Codex
  runs as a separate process and only a <=2k-token handback re-enters Claude's context,
  which is cheaper than even a Claude subagent. Keep small, quick, single-file edits with
- Push the working branch after every commit and before the session ends; a repo without a remote gets one (private GitHub under Jetzu) or a vault git bundle (`/home/vault/v181bb/v181bb10/git_bundles/`) before any further work. Unpushed = unsaved (user ruling 2026-11-07).
  Claude directly — dispatching, gating (`codex-check.sh`) and integrating a Codex job costs
  more turns than writing three lines. Codex writes only into `results/N###-slug/codex/`,
  never the live tree, regardless of which hat it's wearing.
- **control** — **Claude Opus**, or a script where mechanizable. Reads BOTH implementations
  and checks equivalence, plus equivariance for geometric models; or re-derives the key
  number by a DIFFERENT route. Catches the confident-wrong answer. Its independence comes
  from the METHOD, not the model — so same-family is right, a script is better, and
  spending Codex here buys almost nothing. Unaffected by who wrote the code.
- **cross-review (red-team)** — **whichever model did NOT write it.** Claude writes ->
  Codex red-teams (`/codex:rescue`). Codex writes -> Claude red-teams (`/code-review` or a
  general-purpose subagent, same adversarial brief). Attacks the conclusion: the confound,
  the tautology, the leak, the trivial baseline that would score the same. Its independence
  comes from PRIORS, the one thing another model family supplies — a same-family reviewer
  regenerates the confounds its own family already considered. Mandatory, not scoped to
  high-stakes jobs: anything acted on or marked `[verified]` gets cross-reviewed by the
  other model, every time.
- **integrator** — Claude. Checks Codex's code in `results/N###-slug/codex/` against the
  real tree, adapts it to local interfaces and conventions, lands it. The only agent that
  lands Codex code. Never copy blindly: a fix built outside the tree misses local context.
Pair reader+writer per job. Add control and cross-review to anything acted on or written to
KNOWLEDGE as `[verified]`.

## Contract for every subagent
State explicitly: (a) the ONE question or change, (b) its results path
`.agent-research/results/N###-slug/`, (c) "write outputs only there, return <=2k tokens,
cite every number with a path or command", (d) what NOT to touch, (e) if it waits on a
job: one backgrounded blocking call, never a repeated check.
Parallel subagents must not write the same file. Launch independent ones in one message;
serialize anything with a dependency.

## Evidence discipline
- Every number carries its source. No source, no claim.
- A subagent's claim is `[unverified]` until a control or a file read confirms it.
- **Reviewers report; the main agent decides.** Never start a fix on a red-team, control or
  Codex finding you have not reproduced FIRST-HAND — open the cited file:line, rerun the
  cited command, build the trivial baseline it claims would score the same. Only a
  reproduced finding starts the fix. If it does not reproduce, say so in the item and leave
  the code alone: a confident reviewer is still a model, and a false positive costs more
  than the review saved. Both ways — "NOTHING BREAKS" is not proof either, just one search
  that found nothing.
- Name a baseline (the current best) and a stated expected result BEFORE the run; add a kill criterion.
  An attempt may change several things at once (no one-variable rule); ablate only what wins. A result
  without a baseline is not a result.
- Replication: screen on ONE seed against the GOAL.md bar (2 x noise). Run the >= 3-seed replication at the
  END OF EACH MAJOR ACCOMPLISHMENT (a new headline number, before it is called verified, committed or put
  in a PR) — not per candidate, not for every small step.
- Before believing a signal, name the trivial explanation that would produce it anyway
  (constant predictor, tautology, shared clock, warm start) and rule it out.
- Save every measured value (all arms/seeds/metrics/steps, long csv/json) in `results/N###-slug/`
  (>5 MB: cite the external path). 10-24: 139/350 closed exps had numbers only in prose.
- Plot every comparison (`bin/plot-compare`, one per comparison+metric) -> `plots/<metric>_<date>.png`,
  cited in the item. `effect.sh --value` refuses the label without both (void/n/a exempt).

## Waiting on long work
**The cost is the TURN, not the sleep.** A backgrounded call burns nothing and re-invokes
you when it exits; a foreground one spends the turn doing nothing. So: background it.

A PreToolUse hook (`~/.claude/hooks/no-noop-wait.sh`) blocks, in the foreground only:
a command that does nothing (`true`, `:`, filler `echo`), one *described* as a wait that
waits on nothing, one leading with `sleep` under 300s, and a loop polling `squeue`/`sacct`.
It allows anything backgrounded, a sleep used as a settle or timeout inside real work, and
heredoc bodies (writing a watcher script is authoring, not polling). Measured against 14,428
real commands from this machine's history: 3.5% blocked, all of them genuine waits. Blocked?
Background it — relabelling or swapping in a different no-op is what it exists to catch.

History: banning waits by name only relocated the spam (`Bash(true)`, `echo .`). Cheapest pattern first:
1. **Harness-tracked work** (Agent, background Bash, Workflow) — no check at all.
2. **SLURM** — be notified, don't poll. One backgrounded call prints every transition and
   the end state with elapsed + exit code:
       Bash(run_in_background=true): bin/wait-job.sh <jobid> [<jobid>...]
   Exit 0 = all COMPLETED; 1 = a FAILED/TIMEOUT/CANCELLED/OOM job, named in the output.
   Pass every job to ONE waiter, not one waiter each.
3. **Other external state** (CI, a remote queue) — ONE backgrounded blocking call.
4. **A deadline you must tick against** — `ScheduleWakeup`/`/loop`/`Monitor`: 5 min floor,
   20-30 min idle, 1200s+ when something else is the real wake signal. Double after two
   consecutive `noop` ticks — a noop reported nothing, so a longer gap loses nothing.

Name the waiter or the interval in every subagent brief that waits on a job (<=10 min foreground
only — longer jobs are the coordinator's: see 'Several problems at a time').

## Jobs: preempt by default
Helma `preempt` (GPU) / `preempt_cpu`: 1 node, 2 d max, default time 10 min (set `--time`), PreemptMode=
CANCEL (never requeued), 15 min SIGTERM->SIGKILL grace, exempt the first 2 h. Use them unless the job is
multi-node, cannot restart, or has a hard deadline (say which on submit).
- Preempt-safe = resume from latest ckpt, ckpt <=30 min (atomic tmp+rename), save+exit on SIGTERM, keep
  latest+best. Wrap: `exec bin/preempt-run.sh -- <cmd>` (`templates/preempt.sbatch`): on SIGTERM/SIGUSR1
  (`--signal=B:USR1@900`) it resubmits the saved batch script `afterany`, forwards SIGTERM, waits. Options
  in `#SBATCH` lines, parameters in env vars (the command line is not replayed). Tested 10-24 (1120092).
- Mock tests: `bin/preempt-selftest.sh`. `wait-job.sh` follows the chain (`~/.claude/state/preempt-chain/<job>.next`). Stop with
  `bin/preempt-cancel.sh` (plain scancel = SIGTERM = resubmit). wandb: glob logs by job name.
- >25 GPU-h ask: rough estimate from known step times; never a measuring job. Preempt counts too.

## Housekeeping: files and quotas (advisory, every few turns)
Quotas bite on FILE COUNT: /home/hpc ~443k soft/543k hard, /hnvme ~61k/81k (grace, then writes fail -
git, logs, ckpts for every project).
- `bin/quota.sh` (15-min cache); `--warn` prints in state.sh and, at most every 30 min per session, the prompt hook at >=90% soft.
- Big files -> `/hnvme`. Many small TEMP files -> home subdir, deleted at task end. Permanent many-file
  sets: pack (LMDB/tar/HDF5/squashfs). Envs/tools: apptainer `.sif`, no new conda/pip trees.
- Every few turns: delete own stale SLURM logs (metrics synced), wandb dirs, caches, core dumps, superseded
  ckpts, scratch/test output. Look first; own project only.

## Stall guard: 5 flat attempts -> project review
Why: Kale closed ~18 exp items (~13 real attempts) after its TM 0.544 plateau (N042) on width, depth,
seeds, encoders, contact-map refiners; TRIAD_v2 spent N022-N041 (4 HARM, 3 VOID, 1 PARTIAL, 2 thin
wins) on low-t canaries. Both were broken only when the USER typed "big ideas". The guard automates that, at
the user's own patience: a replay of both INDEX files (`evidence/2026-10-08/replay_labels.tsv`, borderline labels
flip verdicts) puts both repos at 9/10 when the user stepped in (TRIAD_v2 strict reading: 52 h earlier). Limit 10 -> 5
on 2026-10-24 (user). MUNDANE would not have fired (their work was module-scale).
- `notebook/GOAL.md` (`bin/goal.sh init`): ONE numeric end metric, target + who set it, best, `noise` = 1 sd of
  identical reruns (measured; source named), constraints. Counting starts at `--since` (default: latest item).
- ONE `exp` item per hypothesis (later jobs go into it); `new-item.sh exp "<title>" knob|module|paradigm`.
- Close an attempt: `bin/effect.sh N### improved|flat|worse --value V | --void` (n/a only `--why infra|measurement`).
  `improved` counts only if V beats `best` by > 2 x noise (the believable single-run delta); else flat.
  Unlabelled closed exp = flat; void = flat; scale `?` counts as knob. Ordered by item ID.
- `bin/stall.sh` counts flat/worse in a row since the last `improved` or closed review. At `stall_limit`:
  state.sh + the per-prompt hook print REVIEW DUE and `new-item.sh exp|task|fix|analysis` is REFUSED until a
  `review` item is open AND its `attempts.md` exists. >= 8 of the last 10 attempts knob-level (MUNDANE): knob/unscaled
  exp refused until opened as module/paradigm. A user-requested run overrides with `STALL_OVERRIDE="<their words>"` (logged).
- REVIEW DUE -> `work-review` skill, autonomous. Close with `bin/review-close.sh N###` (checks attempts/diagnosis/
  ideas/declined files, >= 4 agent reports, >= 3 scale-tagged portfolio exps incl. a paradigm one). Review #2 also tells the user plainly.
- Checked by `bin/selftest.sh` (62 cases, incl. the evidence gate: injection, N1000, races, boundaries, gating). No GOAL.md = guard off.

## Compaction survival
Whatever must outlive the session goes in the notebook, not the transcript: the decision,
its reason, the number, the path. Assume the transcript is gone.

## Two-strike loop: Codex builds in its own folder, Claude integrates
Failure rescue is one trigger for routing a job to Codex, not the only one (see below) —
but it still follows this shape. After TWO failed Claude attempts, stop retrying — two
failures mean the approach is wrong and a third try searches the same priors. Codex DOES
write code here, but never into the live tree, so a real tested implementation crosses over
instead of prose while the repo keeps exactly one writer.
1. **Codex** (`/codex:rescue`): give it the problem, ALL prior attempts and why each
   failed, the files, and its folder. It root-causes, writes and TESTS a fix in
   `results/N###-slug/codex/`, and delivers the plan — what it changed, why, what it could
   not test.
2. **integrator** (Claude): check it against the real tree, adapt, land it.
3. **Claude cross-reviews what LANDED** (`/code-review` or a general-purpose subagent, the
   same adversarial brief Codex uses on Claude's code), not what Codex proposed —
   integration is where fixes break.
4. Still broken? Next round with every prior round attached so it gives NEW ideas. When two
   rounds repeat themselves, stop: that is a stall — run `work-review` (it tells the user plainly).
Log per round: hypothesis, what was tested, and what was wrong with the APPROACH — the
durable lesson, not the diff.

## Codex scope and cadence
Codex quota is ample (2026-10-04): a regular writer AND reviewer. A job routed to Codex enters
Claude's context only as a <=2k-token handback — default it for bulk ports, multi-file work, long
reads; keep quick single-file edits with Claude (a Codex round-trip costs more turns than three
lines). Cross-review is UNCONDITIONAL: the model that did NOT write it red-teams it before it is
acted on or marked `[verified]`, any compute request over 25 GPU-h, and at the end of each two-strike round.

**A Codex job can report `completed` having run nothing.** Verified 2026-09-25: four
rescues were recorded `completed` while bwrap failed on every command
(`max_net_namespaces = 0`; fixed, but the failure mode remains). Never read the status
field as evidence — gate every result:
    bin/codex-check.sh <job-id>          # OK, or CODEX-UNAVAILABLE + exit 2
On `CODEX-UNAVAILABLE` or out-of-quota: do not retry Codex, do not skip — rerun the
red-team with a Claude subagent and write "red-team was same-family (codex unavailable)"
in the item. Weaker coverage beats a `[verified]` bullet nothing ever attacked.

## Invoking Codex
**Default: `bin/codex-run.sh <out-dir> <brief-file> [--ro] [--timeout-min N]`**, called with Bash
`run_in_background: true` (you are re-invoked on exit; no user slash command, no polling). Write the
whole prompt (hat, ONE task, contract, paths) to a brief FILE first - it goes in on stdin, so no
quoting traps. `out-dir` = `results/N###-slug/codex/` = Codex's cwd and only writable root. It
runs plain `codex exec` (no plugin broker, no Sonnet forwarder in between), gates itself, and ends
with one line: `OK ...` (exit 0) or `CODEX-UNAVAILABLE <why>` (exit 2 -> redo with Claude, never
skip). Handback = `<out-dir>/codex_last_message.md`; full stream = `codex_run.jsonl`. Gate = a
finished turn + non-empty handback + no quota/model/sandbox/sqlite failure signature (one retry,
transient infrastructure errors only). Resume a thread: `codex exec resume --last` in the same cwd.

Why not the plugin by default (found 2026-10-17): the
`codex:codex-rescue` forwarder is told "if the Bash call fails, return NOTHING" - an empty reply is
a failure, not "no findings"; it takes `cwd` from whatever it parses out of the prompt (a garbled
path was reported as "Codex CLI is not installed"); and every `task` leaves a broker + app-server
alive holding the NFS sqlite DBs - the SessionEnd hook only tears down the broker of the SESSION's
cwd, so brokers started for other workspaces are orphaned for days (one lived 10 days). Fallback if
you do use it: `/codex:rescue` via the Agent tool (`subagent_type: "codex:codex-rescue"`); treat an
empty return as CODEX-UNAVAILABLE. `/codex:transfer|status|result|cancel` are user-only; Claude can
query with `bin/codex-jobs.sh list | result <job-id> | status [--all]` and gate with `bin/codex-check.sh <job-id>`.
Wrapper `~/.local/bin/codex` now also sets `CODEX_SQLITE_HOME` to node-local `/scratch/.privtmp/<user>/codex-sqlite`
(NFS sqlite locks were the likely cause of the intermittent "failed to initialize sqlite state runtime" -
[unverified], not reproducible in 16 parallel launches).
Always name the hat: **write** (implement a spec, build+test in its folder — regular
implementation work, not just rescue), **red-team** (attack, change nothing), or **fix
round** (root-cause + build in its folder, after two Claude failures). A write job gets the
same contract as any subagent (the ONE task, its results path, what not to touch) plus the
spec or source files it needs.

**What to give a red-team — either direction.** Never "review this". Hand it the claim, the
evidence and the paths, and ask it to break the claim. This applies whether Codex is
red-teaming Claude's code or Claude (via `/code-review` or a general-purpose subagent) is
red-teaming Codex's landed code — same brief, model swapped:
  "Claim: <finding, with its number>. Evidence: <paths / commands / config>.
   Do not fix anything. Find why this claim is wrong:
   (a) what trivial baseline — constant, shuffle, copy of the input — gives this same number?
   (b) is it tautological: does a flag, override or shared schedule force what is measured?
   (c) where could the answer leak into the input?
   (d) is it measured at a flattering point — one step, seed, length, best checkpoint?
   Cite file and line per objection. Say NOTHING BREAKS if you find nothing."
Those four are this project's actual failure history (forced `r_seq=t`; step-2000
measurements on a climbing curve; a collapsed Procrustes mean scoring well; recall read as
precision) — ask them every time, regardless of which model wrote the code under review.

Codex output lands like any subagent's: into the item's `results/` folder, `[unverified]`
until a file read confirms it. The plugin's own job logs live outside the notebook
(`~/.claude/plugins/data/codex-openai-codex/state/`) — copy what mattered in, with the job
id, or it is not a record. A Codex/Claude disagreement is itself evidence worth logging.

1	# BSCCM · Predicting white blood cell markers from label-free images
     2	
     3	Can a microscope image tell us how much of a protein a white blood cell carries, even in a fresh blood sample?
     4	We train an image encoder to predict fluorescence-derived marker levels and use it as a teacher for a second model that reads stained blood smears.
     5	Our primary score, **GOAL**, averages prediction–measurement correlations for 11 targets when we train on one blood draw and test on the other.
     6	Through N088 (24 November 2026), the target is **.700**. The official record is **.6862** (N053, three members, replicated at .6864).
     7	The strongest primary ensemble result so far was **.6911** (N084, four members) against an improvement threshold of **.6916**.
     8	Bright markers associated with cell type transfer well. Dim markers depend strongly on how fluorescence background is estimated.
     9	An external dataset with complete labels shows how much co-expression a model misses when it learns only one marker per cell.

    14	## What one training example contains
    15	
    16	**BSCCM** stands for Berkeley Single Cell Computational Microscopy. It contains **412,941 human white blood cells**.
    17	An LED array illuminates each cell in several ways while a camera records the same crop.
    18	Brightfield shows transmitted light. Darkfield emphasizes light scattered by the cell.
    19	Directional illumination reveals changes in optical phase, which carry information about the cell's internal structure.
    20	Stacking 23 illumination patterns and one computed phase image gives one **24 × 128 × 128** label-free input (LF).
    21	The six fluorescence channels are recorded separately. They supply supervision. [Dataset audit][N001] · [Channel definitions](bsccm/data.py)
    22	
    23	A **surface marker** is a protein on a cell that an antibody can bind. A fluorescent dye attached to the antibody produces a signal that estimates how much of the marker is present.
    24	The targets in this project are transformed fluorescence intensities. A high correlation means that predictions track variation in those measurements.
    25	White blood cell families, or *lineages*, differ in both appearance and protein expression. A model that recognizes lymphocytes, granulocytes and monocytes can therefore predict some variation in a marker without distinguishing two cells of the same type. [Study design][N004] · [Cell-type control][N006]
    26	
    27	| Which cells? | What the microscope measured on the same cell | What this lets us learn |
    28	|---|---|---|
    29	| Single-antibody slide | LF stack, fluorescence for one named protein, autofluorescence estimate | Train that marker head. The other single-marker entries are missing. |
    30	| Pooled or “all” slide | LF stack and fluorescence from a mixture of antibodies, separated into dye groups | Train pooled heads. Antibodies sharing a dye contribute one combined reading. |
    31	| Unstained cells | LF stack and intrinsic fluorescence, also called autofluorescence | Estimate background and learn an auxiliary readout. |
    32	| Wright/Giemsa subset of unstained cells | LF stack, autofluorescence and a registered colour photo after staining | Match an image across modalities and test a student's autofluorescence prediction on the same cell. |
    33	
    34	For orientation, CD3, CD19 and CD56 help identify different lymphocyte populations (T, B and natural killer cells). **Co-expression** asks which markers occur together on an individual cell. A stain such as Wright makes features like the nucleus and granules visible in colour. That morphology can suggest a cell family even when it cannot distinguish two cells with different marker profiles. [Marker and morphology study](.agent-research/results/N002-literature-review-trimodal-alignment-wit/SYNTHESIS.md) · [Measured marker pairs][N080]
    35	
    36	There are **two blood draws**, each divided among slides for different antibody conditions. “Batch” in the data means an isolation, distinct from an optimizer minibatch.
    37	A **field of view** (FOV) is one camera field on a slide and can contain several cells.
    38	Cells from the same field share illumination, background and sample preparation. Cells on the same slide also share a stain and acquisition session.
    39	The release provides draw identity without individual donor IDs. New-draw performance is consequently a two-direction transfer experiment. [Pairing and splits][N004] · [Slide audit][N003]
    40	
    41	A single-stain cell typically has one observed protein plus autofluorescence. After quality control, pooled cells have four observed group targets in draw 0 and three in draw 1, with no autofluorescence target.
    42	The 37,284 pooled-panel cells report groups such as CD3/CD19/CD56, a dye shared by three antibodies.
    43	The combined intensity cannot distinguish a CD3-bright cell from a CD19-bright cell with the same total signal.
    44	Only some pooled cells of draw 0 have **gates** (cell-type assignments derived from measured signals).
    45	No BSCCM cell has two separately measured *single-stain* markers. An output vector with a prediction in every column is easy to produce. Its within-cell pattern is much harder to validate. [Dataset design][N004] · [Joint-decoding review][N079]
    46	
    47	The **15,712 Wright/Giemsa photos** (GS in code) correspond to 10,015 LF cells from draw 0 and 5,697 from draw 1.
    48	Every one comes from an antibody-unstained slide. There are **zero same-cell GS–surface-marker pairs**.
    49	LF bridges the datasets. We can teach a Giemsa network to imitate the LF teacher on paired images, then test it against measured autofluorescence.
    50	A marker estimate reached by this route depends on assumptions about what the LF image captured.
    51	In particular, a marker and the Giemsa image might share information even after conditioning on LF. The project cannot test that assumption from the two sets of pairs alone. [Premise audit][N004] · [Simulation][N016] · [Error estimates][N017]
    52	
    53	### Why bring in other datasets?
    54	
    55	| Dataset | Available observations | Role in the experiments |
    56	|---|---|---|
    57	| PBC | 17,092 clinical peripheral blood smear images with expert cell-class labels | Adapt the GS reader with common cell classes on half A. Test marker rankings on disjoint half B, including classes withheld from adaptation. |
    58	| MLL23 | Clinical smear images with class labels, including finer blood-cell populations | External comparison of predicted marker rankings. No MLL23 cells enter training or alignment. Repeated use to compare methods makes it a development benchmark. |
    59	| S-BIAD452 | ImageStream imaging flow cytometry, 274,050 cells, three donors. Two brightfield images and side scatter as input, nine antibody measurements per cell | Hide different subsets of a known marker vector during training. Compare full and sparse supervision on a held-out donor where all nine true values are available. |
    60	
    61	PBC and MLL23 test an *ordering*. For example, how often does a neutrophil receive a higher CD16 prediction than an eosinophil?
    62	The images and class labels support this test even when individual marker concentrations are unavailable.
    63	ImageStream supports a different question. The nine markers are CD15, Siglec8, CD14, CD19, CD3, CD45, CD4, CD56 and CD8. Their target levels are derived from background-subtracted fluorescence images on all donors. Five of its markers overlap with BSCCM (CD3, CD14, CD19, CD45 and CD56), and all nine are measured together, allowing a direct test of correlations between markers. [PBC audit][N008] · [MLL23 contrasts][N022] · [External data audit][N077] · [Donor protocol][N080]

    65	## What counts as progress
    66	
    67	1. **Choose a direction.** `b10` means train on draw 1 and test on draw 0. `b01` reverses them. The GOAL fine-tunes use eligible source-draw rows and score split 2 (held-out FOVs) of the other draw. GS rows are excluded. A separate `fov` experiment trains on split 0 and tests on split 2 across both draws. It answers an easier question. [Split implementation](scripts/train_lf.py)
    68	2. **Exclude the test draw from self-supervised learning (SSL).** SSL learns from unlabelled images before marker fine-tuning. Each direction gets its own encoder initialization. Historical LF flat-field calibration uses unlabelled slide statistics, including test slides. Model training and instrument calibration therefore have different data boundaries. [Inductive control][N031] · [Calibration audit][N053]
    69	3. **Score each target on observed cells.** Compute Pearson's correlation coefficient, *r*, between predictions and measurements using the target's mask. Average the 11 correlations with equal weight, then average the two directions with equal weight. For an ensemble, align cell rows and average member predictions **before** calculating correlations. [Common-11 scorer](scripts/score_goal_arms.py) · [Ensemble scorer](.agent-research/results/N053-lf-encoder-swap-on-the-v10-goal-dinov3-v/n053_score.py)
    70	4. **Track the three pooled targets separately.** **MM3** averages the three pooled-target correlations over both directions. A cell-type-only predictor reached .730 on pooled targets in the reviewed b01 test. MM3 can improve while biologically important marker pairs remain unresolved within a type. [MM3 replication][N083] · [Cell-type baseline][N079]
    71	5. **Freeze the question before looking at the result.** The experiment record specifies the primary comparison, label file, baseline and success threshold. The estimated GOAL seed standard deviation is **.0027**. “Improved” requires a gain **greater than twice that noise**, currently a score **above .6916**. A positive difference below the bar is *flat*. A secondary combination can guide the next experiment. [Rules](.agent-research/notebook/RULES.md) · [Noise and threshold](.agent-research/notebook/GOAL.md)
    72	
    73	The **common 11** are eight single proteins (CD16, CD14, CD45, CD3, CD123, CD56, HLA-DR and CD19)
    74	and three pooled targets (`grp:CD3/CD19/CD56`, `grp:CD45`, `grp:CD16`).
    75	The regression head has 13 outputs. Autofluorescence is auxiliary. A fourth pooled target, `grp:CD123/HLA-DR/CD14`, failed quality control on one draw.
    76	Those last two outputs carry no GOAL weight. A blank target has no training loss. [Target definitions](scripts/make_targets_v5.py) · [Figure 6 caption](figures/overview/CAPTIONS.md)

    94	## What worked for each task
    95	
    96	Three learning methods recur across the comparisons. In **distillation**, a student learns to reproduce a teacher’s outputs or internal representation. **Optimal transport** matches two distributions under a cost for moving one observation toward another. **Conditional flow matching** learns how to transform noise into samples compatible with a given image. Only the first requires a teacher, and matching a distribution alone does not identify an individual cell. [GS student][N010] · [Transport experiment][N045] · [Flow experiment][N034]

   115	## Reproduce the marker ensembles
   116	
   117	### Architecture and training recipe
   118	
   119	| Member | What it sees | Initialization and fine-tuning |
   120	|---|---|---|
   121	| N048 full view | ResNet-50, 128 × 128, 2,048 pooled features | In-domain SSL, then marker supervision on cofactor-150 labels. |
   122	| N048 centre zoom | A second ResNet-50, central 64 × 64 resampled to 128 × 128 | Same direction-specific SSL checkpoint, separate fine-tune on cofactor-150 labels. |
   123	| N053 Cytoland | ConvNeXtV2-T, 768 features, learned gain per channel | Published VSCyto2D microscopy encoder. Adapt its one-channel stem to 24 inputs and use 0.1× encoder learning rate. Fine-tune on v10. |
   124	| N084 addition | ConvNeXt-S, 768 features, full view | In-domain SSL for 60 epochs on draw 1 or 120 on draw 0, followed by a v10 fine-tune with seed 1. |
   125	
   126	The full-view ResNet has 23.6M parameters, Cytoland 27.9M and ConvNeXt-S 49.5M.
   127	For in-domain SSL, draw two augmented views of an unlabelled source cell, encourage their projections to agree, and regularize the projected distribution toward a Gaussian with SIGReg to avoid collapse.
   128	The ResNets use 40 SSL epochs. At fine-tuning, pool the encoder features and fit 13 linear outputs with masked mean squared error.
   129	Auxiliary 3- and 10-class heads use cross-entropy with classification weight 0.5 on eligible gated cells. Inference uses the regression outputs.
   130	Train for 10 epochs with AdamW and a one-cycle learning-rate schedule peaking at 0.0005, batch size 256 and random shifts up to four pixels.
   131	Rotating a crop would change which physical illumination direction a channel describes, so the record recipe uses translations.

   337	### Running jobs
   338	
   339	The cluster uses SLURM. The generic CPU wrapper requests a 48-core NUMA fraction on `preempt_cpu`. Packing parallelizes over cell blocks.
   340	The training wrapper requests one GPU and 16 host cores on `preempt`, binds the workspace into the container, and invokes Python with the contents of `CMD`.
   341	Jobs can be preempted. The training wrapper uses the work-log preemption helper and resumable checkpoints.
   342	A restarted job can receive a new SLURM ID, so check that the final encoder file exists before using it in a dependent run. [CPU wrapper](scripts/cpu_job.sbatch) · [Packing job](scripts/pack.sbatch) · [GPU wrapper](scripts/gpu_job.sbatch) · [N078 resubmissions](.agent-research/results/N078-in-domain-ssl-scaling-sigreg-lf-pretrain/jobs.txt)
   343	
   344	The project uses GPUs when the task is at least twice as fast as a well-parallelized CPU run. Estimate the total GPU-hours before submitting a training sweep. A sweep above 25 GPU-hours needs project approval.
   345	Record each training submission in its experiment item, including config, job ID, budget and log path, and register its offline Weights & Biases run and sync lineage.
   346	Compute nodes have no internet. The login-node cron syncs offline metrics. Completed runs also leave local results and predictions. [Project context](.agent-research/results/N088-literature-review-user-11-24-label-free/context.md) · [Sync script](scripts/wandb_sync_cron.sh)

   358	### Establish the dataset and the two measurable links
   359	
   360	**[N001] · Pack and verify the release.** Converted the 50 checksum-verified Dryad chunks into indexed memory-mapped arrays for 412,941 cells.
   361	Independent decoding found zero mismatched arrays in the sampled records. The pack became the common input format.
   362	
   363	**[N002] · Literature review, learning through a shared modality.** Reviewed six strands of work on partial pairings, transfer and evaluation.
   364	The review proposed hiding known pairs in a simulation to test transitive error estimates. The two real paired datasets alone could not establish GS marker accuracy. [Review synthesis](.agent-research/results/N002-literature-review-trimodal-alignment-wit/SYNTHESIS.md)
   365	
   366	**[N003] · Audit the LF–GS matches.** Areas measured independently from matched Wright and LF phase images had Spearman correlation .740 versus .000 after shuffling.
   367	Pairing was informative but imperfect. The outlier analysis gave a rough upper estimate around 7% for mismatches and heavy-tailed residuals together.
   368	
   369	**[N004] · Change the project design after auditing the pairing.** All 15,712 GS cells belonged to antibody-unstained slides.
   370	With zero GS–marker pairs, use LF as the bridge and distinguish measured same-cell endpoints from inferred marker agreement.
   371	
   372	**[N005] · Build masked targets and calibrate the images.** Constructed 13 outputs with masks, draw-specific controls and gated cell classes.
   373	Flat-field correction reduced brightfield background–radius correlation from −.435 to −.040. Preserve illumination direction during augmentation.
   374	
   375	### First LF models and the spatial confound
   376	
   377	**[N006] · Supervised ResNet-18 baseline.** On v3, mean r over 12 marker targets was .707 on held-out FOVs and .494/.471 across draws.
   378	A three-class mean predictor matched or beat the network on several gated pooled targets. Cell type explained much of the initial signal.
   379	
   380	**[N007] · Self-supervised pretraining.** Tested two views of a cell with disjoint illumination channels against augmentation-only views.
   381	Frozen augmentation-only probes reached .486/.472 across draws versus .460/.435 for disjoint illumination. The stronger SSL recipe went forward to fine-tuning.
   382	
   383	**[N008] · Test an external cell-type anchor.** A PBC classifier with .988 in-domain accuracy called 72–75% of the BSCCM Wright cells platelets.
   384	In-domain GS clusters agreed with LF-predicted broad classes on .858 of cells. The PBC classifier did not transfer directly.
   385	
   386	**[N009] · Bind frozen GS and marker encoders to LF.** The first fused model retrieved the exact LF cell among ten candidates only .011 of the time on the held-out GS slide.
   387	Simpler linear contrastive alignment reached .349 within a slide and .033 across slides. Early raw-autofluorescence comparisons were revisited after N012.
   388	
   389	**[N010] · Train the Giemsa image encoder.** Fine-tuning the last four DinoBloom blocks with stain augmentation, normalization or adversarial training yielded raw-autofluorescence r .284–.308 on the first held-out slide.
   390	On later detrended targets the student reached .648/.323 across slides versus its LF teacher's .559/.305.
   391	
   392	**[N011] · Diagnose slide shift.** A classifier identified the slide with .920 accuracy from GS features and .990 from LF features.
   393	Direct GS regression on raw autofluorescence fell from about .620 within slide to .440–.450 across slides, prompting a spatial control.
   394	
   395	**[N012] · Test position alone.** A region-blocked position model predicted raw autofluorescence and CD19 with median r .840 each.
   396	It also predicted CD56 (.530) and CD123 (.490). Spatial backgrounds confounded several apparent biological signals.
   397	
   398	**[N013] · Detrend the labels, v4.** Removed each slide's position trend from the targets and flagged 567 suspect image pairs.
   399	ResNet-18 reached .555 across draws on the 12-target metric. The FOV-to-draw gap shrank from about .220 to .080.
   400	
   401	**[N014] · Fine-tune the SSL encoder as a marker teacher.** On v4 the pretrained ResNet-50 reached .574 versus .565 for ResNet-50 trained from scratch.
   402	Adversarial draw invariance gave .554 for the ResNet-18 arm. Fine-tuning recovered value that the frozen probes missed.
   403	
   404	**[N015] · Pass the improved teacher to the GS student.** The student distilled from the stronger LF marker model scored .641/.303 on detrended autofluorescence across the two slides.
   405	Improving the LF marker task gave no corresponding improvement on the GS autofluorescence endpoint.
   406	
   407	**[N016] · Test the bridge where ground truth is available.** Split LF illumination channels into two artificial modalities and hid the direct pairs.
   408	Error bounds covered 95% of comparisons. Distilled r .457–.488 was close to the direct oracle .465 in this same-instrument simulation.
   409	
   410	**[N017] · Estimate GS marker error on real cells.** Combined student–teacher correlation and teacher–measurement correlation under a calibrated-teacher and conditional-independence assumption.
   411	For draw 0 → 1 this estimated CD16 at .800 and CD123 at .170. The measured GS autofluorescence check was .649. Only the latter has same-cell truth.
   412	
   413	**[N018] · Map information to illumination patterns.** On held-out FOVs, brightfield alone gave .585 across 12 targets, all darkfield .619 and the full stack .635.
   414	CD123 specifically gave .384 from darkfield versus .390 from the full stack. The map was evaluated within draws.
   415	
   416	### Transfer the GS student and repair the labels
   417	
   418	**[N019] · Test the GS student on clinical PBC smears.** Zero-shot marker rankings varied widely. CD16 for neutrophils versus eosinophils gave AUROC .107, while the CD14 monocyte contrast gave .709.
   419	The direct transfer failed several pre-specified biological orderings.
   420	
   421	**[N020] · Adapt using unlabelled PBC images.** Adapted on half A and tested on half B. Mean AUROC was .406 unadapted, .438 after whitening and .462/.555 with the two adversarial weights.
   422	Individual contrasts could reverse. Distribution matching gave no consistent clinical gain. [PBC contrast values](.agent-research/results/N020-clinical-transfer-via-unsupervised-domai/pbc_transfer_auroc.csv) · [Reviewed comparison](figures/overview/fig9_alignment_domain.png)
   423	
   424	**[N021] · Add common-class anchors.** Trained against labelled PBC neutrophils, lymphocytes and monocytes. Anchor-related comparisons scored .790–1.000 but partly reused the fitted class structure.
   425	For the unanchored eosinophil CD16 contrast, AUROC was .950 and .360 on two seeds. Finer transfer remained unstable.
   426	
   427	**[N022] · Give rare cells more training weight.** Tail weighting and a focal-loss gate head raised in-draw FOV r from .654 to .674.
   428	MLL23 fine-contrast AUROC was .494 for the tail-weighted chain versus .630 for the earlier ResNet-18 reference. The in-draw gain failed to transfer.
   429	
   430	**[N023] · Repair a pooled assay and re-base on v5.** Draw-1 pooled CD123/HLA-DR/CD14 failed dye and cell-type controls. Dropping it and changing normalization took frozen predictions from .574 to .6343.
   431	Training on repaired labels then gave .640 against a matched .6346. Only the latter comparison measures training progress.
   432	
   433	**[N024] · Trace the v5 labels through the GS chain.** Within-slide GS autofluorescence rose from .383/.689 to .510/.867.
   434	MLL23 fine-contrast AUROC fell from .622 to .536. The same-cell proxy and external clinical ranking favored different teachers.
   435	
   436	**[N025] · Use separate teachers for different readouts.** TT6 used a v4 marker teacher and a v6 autofluorescence teacher trained with unstained-slide autofluorescence.
   437	GS autofluorescence was .578/.855 and MLL23 AUROC .611 versus the v4 chain's .622. Clinical non-inferiority remained unresolved, and review identified a target-calibration leak.
   438	
   439	**[N026] · Model the cell at two scales.** Averaging a full-view and 2× zoomed ResNet reached .651/.652 on v5 using SSL that included unlabelled images of both draws.
   440	A same-scale full-view ensemble gave .6438. Re-estimating batch-normalization statistics on the test draw reduced r by .005–.011.
   441	
   442	**[N027] · Increase Giemsa-student capacity.** More trainable blocks and more steps reduced MLL23 fine-contrast AUROC from .611 to .529 with DinoBloom-B and .420 with DinoBloom-L.
   443	Additional capacity failed to improve same-cell truth or clinical transfer.
   444	
   445	**[N028] · Generate virtual Wright images from LF.** Trained on registered LF–GS pairs. Structural image similarity on the two held-out slides was .872/.865.

   691	## Current work and open questions
   692	
   693	**Can the ensemble clear .6916 on the frozen v10 protocol?** N085 combines 120-epoch source-only ConvNeXt-S pretraining on both draws with panel heads for pooled targets and two-part/FOV-offset heads for singles.
   694	Its primary comparison is the pre-specified eight-member average. MM3, the six-member subset and standalone members are secondary. The item records the work as running. [N085] · [Registered scorer](.agent-research/results/N085-stronger-members-convnext-s-with-120-ep/n085_score.py)
   695	
   696	**Can the decoder recover more from a fixed image?** N087 starts with the same ResNet features and compares the original head, ridge regression, reduced-rank readouts, a multilayer perceptron and nearest neighbours.
   697	A recovered baseline of .6730 checks that the feature export and scoring agree with the original model. The proposed nonlinear follow-up requires gains above .0054 in both directions. [N087]
   698	
   699	**What survives compression?** The image autoencoder arm trains on the source draw with latent sizes 16, 64 and 256. Held-out performance is measured by GOAL, clustering agreement with gated classes, and nearest-neighbour balanced accuracy.
   700	PCA-compressed SSL features provide a matched-dimension control. Other arms retain the pretrained SSL projector or add a narrow bottleneck during fine-tuning. [N087]
   701	
   702	**Can a model learn realistic marker combinations for an ambiguous image?** A marker autoencoder or PCA learns a prior on complete profiles from a separate donor.
   703	The sandbox asks whether this reduces 36-pair error to .210 or less with at most .010 loss in macro r. A conditional flow arm samples a whole nine-marker vector from an image embedding.
   704	It compares predicted pair correlations, CD4/CD8 exclusivity and population fractions against a mean-squared-error decoder on identical features. A follow-up with sparse labels depends on the jointly labelled test. [N087]
   705	
   706	**Can a class-conditional match help Giemsa cells?** N087 also proposes class means and within-class optimal transport from GS embeddings to marker profiles.
   707	Teacher agreement, measured autofluorescence and clinical contrasts remain the available endpoints. Direct GS–marker accuracy still requires a paired reference. [N087] · [Pairing audit][N004]
   708	
   709	**Which comparisons are genuinely new?** N088 reviews LF-to-marker prediction, learned projections and autoencoders, sparse multi-target supervision, marker priors and cross-modal alignment.
   710	The idea backlog includes a zoomed ConvNeXt-S member, ImageStream pretraining with separate downstream heads, and testing bag-level learning on cohorts with varying cell composition.
   711	A proposal for the supervising lab is to acquire marker and Wright images on the same cells. Those pairs could test the GS bridge directly and help adjudicate proxy-label disagreement. These are proposals, with outcomes still to be measured. [N088] · [Open ideas](.agent-research/notebook/IDEAS.md)

# N088 synthesis: three literature reviews (A label-free/representations, B sparse multi-target, C alignment/shift), 104 references
## What the literature says about our open questions
- Autoencoder latents cluster cell identity worse than SSL in every microscopy comparison (cytoself without its identity pretext 3-5x
  worse; Lu et al. 2019 AE 42.5 % vs SSL 88.0 % kNN) and small bottlenecks keep illumination/background variance (A). -> N087 AE arm is a
  test, not a hope.
- Post-projector features are worse than backbone features; SIGReg makes the projector output isotropic (no clusters by design) (A).
- Distribution alignment (DANN/OT/CORAL) provably fails when class proportions differ between domains (Zhao et al. ICML 2019) (C) ->
  explains N014/N026/N056.
- The within-slide LF<->Giemsa retrieval (.38-.40) may be a field-of-view shortcut (~3 paired cells per field) (C) -> audit.
- The only unused information channel in BSCCM training is each cell's own measured marker (B); external joint data is the only source
  of cross-marker structure (B).
- Feature-preserving fine-tuning (LP-FT, lower encoder LR, WiSE-FT) is the one lever both A and C rate highest for a 2-draw shift and
  that was never applied to our in-domain SSL encoders (Kumar et al. ICLR 2022; Wortsman et al. CVPR 2022). In-house evidence: Cytoland
  encoder LR x0.1 .6671 vs x1.0 .6464 (N053).
## Portfolio (GPU-h; status)
1. N090 gentle fine-tuning of SSL ResNet-50: encoder LR x0.1 / x0.3 (2 seeds x 2 directions, ~3 h; launched), then LP-FT + WiSE-FT
   interpolation (Codex code). Pre-registered bar +.0054 over control .6706 (2-seed mean).
2. N087 (running): decoder sweep, image AE, marker prior, flow decoder (done: no co-expression gain), equal-label-count control (B).
3. Missing-marker completion from the measured marker (B-P1): free CPU gate in the sandbox, then ~5-6 h.
4. Field-of-view shortcut audit (C-P1, CPU), then nuisance-aware LF<->Giemsa alignment (~2.5 h) only if the audit confirms it.
5. Nested (Matryoshka) projection head (A-P2, sandbox first, ~2-3 h) replaces N087-D3 (narrow backbone, predicted harmful).
6. Cell-type mixture head with S-BIAD452 profiles (B-P2, ~3 h) after the equal-label-count control.
7. DINO-style in-domain SSL (A-P3, ~6 h) and cross-slide positives in SSL (C-P3, ~4 h): diverse ensemble members.

## Reproduce the marker ensembles

### Architecture and training recipe

| Member | What it sees | Initialization and fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|
| N048 full view | ResNet-50, 128 × 128, 2,048 pooled features | In-domain SSL, then marker supervision on cofactor-150 labels. |
| N048 centre zoom | A second ResNet-50, central 64 × 64 resampled to 128 × 128 | Same direction-specific SSL checkpoint, separate fine-tune on cofactor-150 labels. |
| N053 Cytoland | ConvNeXtV2-T, 768 features, learned gain per channel | Published VSCyto2D microscopy encoder. Adapt its one-channel stem to 24 inputs and use 0.1× encoder learning rate. Fine-tune on v10. |
| N084 addition | ConvNeXt-S, 768 features, full view | In-domain SSL for 60 epochs on draw 1 or 120 on draw 0, followed by a v10 fine-tune with seed 1. |

The full-view ResNet has 23.6M parameters, Cytoland 27.9M and ConvNeXt-S 49.5M.
For in-domain SSL, draw two augmented views of an unlabelled source cell, encourage their projections to agree, and regularize the projected distribution toward a Gaussian with SIGReg to avoid collapse.
The ResNets use 40 SSL epochs. At fine-tuning, pool the encoder features and fit 13 linear outputs with masked mean squared error.
Auxiliary 3- and 10-class heads use cross-entropy with classification weight 0.5 on eligible gated cells. Inference uses the regression outputs.
Train for 10 epochs with AdamW and a one-cycle learning-rate schedule peaking at 0.0005, batch size 256 and random shifts up to four pixels.
Rotating a crop would change which physical illumination direction a channel describes, so the record recipe uses translations.
[Architecture caption](figures/overview/CAPTIONS.md) · [Teacher code](scripts/train_lf.py) · [View construction](bsccm/ssl.py)

### Start with the saved predictions

On the project cluster the packed data, weights and saved predictions already have the paths expected by the scripts.
The following Bash commands run from the repository root. They need NumPy and pandas and write only into a fresh output directory.
The example uses the cluster’s CPU Python environment. Training uses the Apptainer image.

```bash
cd "$HOME/BSCCM"
repo=$PWD
W=/hnvme/workspace/v181bb10-bsccm
out=$(mktemp -d)
py=("$HOME/miniforge3/envs/triad/bin/python" -I)

# Check all positions in the two directions before calculating a mean.
for member in n048_v9_base n048_v9_zoom2 n053_cytoland n053_cytoland_s1 n051_v10_base; do
  for d in b10 b01; do
    test -s "$W/runs/${member}_${d}/eval_preds.npz" || exit 1
  done
done
for member in n083_cnxs60_s1_b10 n084_cnxs120_s1_b01; do
  test -s "$W/runs/$member/eval_preds.npz" || exit 1
done

# Single models. Each arm names a run prefix without its _b10 or _b01 suffix.
"${py[@]}" scripts/score_goal_arms.py "$out" \
  control=n048_v9_base zoom=n048_v9_zoom2 cytoland=n053_cytoland

# N053 averages saved predictions row by row, then scores the common 11.
"${py[@]}" .agent-research/results/N053-*/n053_score.py "$out/n053.csv" \
  n048_v9_base+n048_v9_zoom2+n053_cytoland \
  n048_v9_base+n048_v9_zoom2+n053_cytoland_s1

# N084 uses different ConvNeXt-S run names for the two directions.
# Its scorer writes n084_scores.csv in the current directory.
(cd "$out" && "${py[@]}" "$repo"/.agent-research/results/N084-*/n084_score.py)
```

`eval_preds.npz` contains a prediction matrix `P` and global cell-row IDs `G`.
The N053 scorer verifies the same row order across members. Every scorer above reads **v10** measurements for those IDs.
In `score_goal_arms.py`, comma-separated runs are replicate **seeds**. It writes `goal_arms.csv` (target-level), `goal_summary.csv` and `plot_goal.csv`.
Use the N053 scorer's **plus-separated** syntax for an ensemble. The fine-tuner's generic validation mean can include a different set of columns. [Arm scorer](scripts/score_goal_arms.py) · [N053 scorer](.agent-research/results/N053-lf-encoder-swap-on-the-v10-goal-dinov3-v/n053_score.py) · [N084 scorer](.agent-research/results/N084-pre-registered-ensemble-confirmation-n05/n084_score.py)

| Expected check on saved predictions | Draw 1 → 0 | Draw 0 → 1 | GOAL | MM3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| N053, three members | .7001 | .6723 | .6862 | .7734 |
| N053, retrain only Cytoland with seed 1 | .7043 | .6685 | .6864 | — |
| N084, add ConvNeXt-S to seed-0 N053 | .7030 | .6793 | .6911 | .7764 |
